evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The MOE entry identifies 𠀃 as a variant of 几 and says the form occurs under 且 in the Duan commentary to Shuowen, where it is described as an ancient form used for both 且 and 几. The MOE record does not describe 𠀃 as an earlier ancestor of 几; it also marks many ancient-script references unavailable. Thus the dossier's claim that 𠀃 was the original form and that its bottom stroke depicts ground is not established by this inspected source.

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The entry gives the Shuowen account for 幾: '微也。殆也。从𢆶从戍。戍，兵守也。𢆶而兵守者，危也。' It separately records meanings with literary citations, including subtle sign/indication, slight/few, near/almost, danger, interrogative how many, and uses equivalent to 機. These cited examples are not a complete chronological chain, and the Shuowen analysis is a historical account rather than independent confirmation of the formation.
evidence.title: [A01200] 幾 - Ministry of Education Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants

evidence.field: Glyph origin; pronunciation and historical phonology; meaning
evidence.text: The entry presents 几 as a pictograph of a small stool seen from the side and asserts 𠀃 as its original form, with the bottom stroke interpreted as floor/ground. Its glyph-history table has labels for Warring States, Shuowen small seal, and Ming Liushutong, but the retrieved text does not expose glyph images for visual verification. It records modern Mandarin jī and jǐ, Cantonese gei1/gei2; Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese /*C.kr[ə]jʔ/ and Zhengzhang Old Chinese /*krilʔ/ for the stool reading; and the Book of Rites example 操几杖 in a text described there as c. 4th–2nd century BCE. The separate interrogative/quantity reading is assigned to 幾, whose modern simplified spelling is 几. The Proto-Sino-Tibetan comparison is an asserted word-etymology proposal; the source provides no independently recoverable pronunciation for a depicted stool object that would prove an object-name borrowing.
evidence.title: 几 - Wiktionary

evidence.text: For the independent stool character 几, this page reports Middle Chinese kjijX and Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese /*C.kr[ə]jʔ/; Zhengzhang /*krilʔ/. These are competing reconstruction systems, not variants to merge. The stool graph's pronunciation and meaning do not make 几 a phonetic component in itself; the dossier's cited material does not offer evidence for a sound role within 几.

evidence.field: 几 entry; glyph definition and commentary
evidence.text: The entry reproduces Shuowen’s description of 几 as a pictograph and its list of ritual furniture. Duan Yucai’s commentary corrects 踞 to 凥 and describes a raised, flat top with a support below; this is a historical interpretation, not independent proof of the graph’s original referent.

search_audit.outcome: Searched the web and inspected the MOE 几 and 幾 entries and the Wiktionary 几 entry. The MOE 几 page records 𠀃 as a variant and cites a Shuowen/Duan note, but does not establish chronological precedence or a ground-stroke interpretation. The MOE 幾 page supplies the Shuowen account and lexical citations. Wiktionary's extracted text describes ancient-form categories but did not render their images for inspection. Attempts to open the Ctext 几 and 幾 pages returned internal errors.

search_audit.outcome: Search surfaced the Shuowen-derived entry, the MOE variant record, CUHK dictionary entry and secondary glyph claims. Opened source pages. Ctext returned 403; no relevant Commons file or accessible Xiaoxuetang record/direct image was established.
Search returned the official database home and general record pages but no exact usable 几 glyph record. The supplied failed image URL was not retried.

gaps: No glyph images were visually inspected. Therefore the claimed ancient shape evolution of 几, including whether its lower stroke depicts ground and whether the graph depicts a stool, remains an account reported by sources rather than an independently checked visual conclusion.

The MOE variant entry supports 𠀃 as a variant of 几, but the reviewed material does not determine whether this is an earlier form, a nonchronological alternative, or a related graph later associated with 几. Do not caption it as an original/ancestor without further evidence.

No verified early dated artifact or contextual text for the stool graph was retrieved. The Book of Rites citation supports an older textual use but does not itself date the graph's invention or establish the semantic path from stool to table.

The proposed Proto-Sino-Tibetan comparison and alleged stool-word relationship lack sufficient inspected primary evidence here. A reconstruction for a related word cannot establish the original spoken name of the depicted object; no object-name borrowing conclusion is supported.

No evidence retrieved establishes when the interrogative/quantity uses written 几 began. Modern simplified 几 represents traditional 幾 in those senses; the graphics and lexemes must remain distinguished from the independent stool graph 几.

No phonetic component is proposed for 几. Its own pronunciation is not evidence of a component role. Baxter–Sagart and Zhengzhang forms reported above are distinct systems; the repository Baxter–Sagart TSV was not independently matched to exact rows or linked to a verified official upstream source page in this research response.

No selected glyph image: external searches and inspected pages did not establish a usable direct image with verified identity and reuse provenance. The supplied Xiaoxuetang image request had returned 401 and was excluded as required.
No glyph pixels were visually inspected. The table/stool interpretation is a traditional dictionary account; the claimed 𠀃 ground stroke and ancestor status remain unverified.

The reviewed sources do not establish a dated earliest occurrence of 几 or a chronological semantic path from stool to table. The Shuowen furniture citation is not evidence for the graph’s invention date.

No evidence supports the proposed Proto-Sino-Tibetan comparison or an object-name borrowing claim. The stool graph is treated here as an independent pictographic analysis, not as a phonetic component or demonstrated whole-graph loan.
